# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative; prospective]
Catalyst, solvent, temperature, and reaction time are categorical/continuous determinants of conversion and selectivity; extraction identity and organic-phase handling determine whether reaction yield becomes final recovery. With no dossier, indices carry no ordering. Initial batches will deliberately screen categories and conditions.

**Prospective expectation:** a complete heated, catalyzed reaction followed by quench, organic extraction, settling, retention of the organic phase, washing, concentration and drying should yield assayable product. I expect at least one catalyst/solvent combination to exceed purity 0.80, but the winning categories and temperature are unresolved. An intermediate HPLC observation will be used in each batch to distinguish reaction limitations from workup losses; this claim would change if product preferentially reports in the aqueous phase or heating mainly raises degradation.

## Decisions
Use all 12 batches and exactly one nonfinal measurement per batch. Treat final-assay recovery/purity as authoritative; do not infer ordering from anonymous indices.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only as a screening lead]
At 340 K for 3600 s with otherwise matched 0.04 mol charge, 0.04 L solvent, 0.005 mol catalyst, catalyst-C1/solvent-S1 gave the strongest observed reaction-stage HPLC response so far (conversion ~0.30, selectivity ~0.50, yield ~0.16; event runner-operation-0024). The other tested paired category recipes were lower in stage yield/selectivity (events runner-operation-0040, -0056, -0072). Because catalyst, solvent and extractant changed together in the first comparisons, individual causal effects remain unresolved.

## H2 [unresolved]
The standard workup (aqueous addition, 0.04 L extraction, organic retention, one 0.04 L wash, drying) substantially raises purity but loses target. Final assays through batch 5 show recovery only about 0.026–0.044 and purity 0.57–0.77 (events runner-operation-0034, -0050, -0066, -0082). Numerical differences suggest X1 is a promising extractant category, but it is confounded with the best reaction recipe and uncertainty/repeatability do not yet justify a category-effect claim. No completed batch yet meets purity >=0.80.

## H3 [revised]
Post-extraction concentration is suspended: batch 1 gave zero reported recovery after two concentration steps (runner-operation-0018), whereas non-concentrated comparable workups retained measurable recovery. This is observational and confounded, but the downside is large enough to avoid concentration unless later evidence contradicts it.

## Next tests
Center further combinations around C1, S1 and X1 while changing one or two categories. If purity remains just below 0.80, test additional washing while tracking the recovery tradeoff.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in the screened scope]
For 340 K, 3600 s reactions, C1/S1 repeatedly produced stage HPLC selectivity around 0.49–0.54 and yield around 0.14–0.17 (events runner-operation-0024, -0088, -0104, -0120, -0136, -0153). This repeatability supports the combination as a reaction-stage lead, although final workup purity for its tested extracts remained below 0.80.

## H2 [supported tradeoff, mechanism unresolved]
Workup increased purity but caused substantial target loss. Varying X0–X3 under repeated C1/S1 conditions gave final purity near 0.77–0.78 and recovery about 0.033–0.051 (final-assay events runner-operation-0098, -0114, -0130; with X1 at runner-operation-0034). X2 gave the largest observed recovery in that subset, but category effects remain modest relative to assay uncertainty and run-to-run reaction variation. Repeating washes did not monotonically improve purity and reduced recovery in the three-wash run (runner-operation-0165), so multiple washes are not recommended.

## H3 [supported decision]
Solvent-S0 with C1, X2, 340 K/3600 s and one wash is the only completed recipe whose point-estimate purity clearly exceeds the 0.80 specification: purity 0.8254 and recovery 0.0189 (runner-operation-0181; stated assay standard uncertainties 0.008 and 0.01). Extending the same reaction to 7200 s increased stage yield but final purity fell to 0.7430 (runner-operation-0197), so longer reaction is rejected for the constrained objective.

## Final decision
Recommend completed batch 11. It sacrifices recovery relative to several sub-specification batches, but it is the sole observed compliant batch and its purity margin (~0.025) is larger than the assay purity standard uncertainty. This decision would change if replicate confirmation placed batch 11 below 0.80 or if a near-threshold higher-recovery recipe (especially batch 7 or 9) were independently shown to meet the purity constraint.

payload.report:
MECHANISM REPORT

1. Scope and interpretation

This is an anonymous synthetic reaction–extraction–purification world. Catalyst-C0 through C3, solvent-S0 through S3, and extractant-X0 through X3 are independent categorical labels; the campaign provides no basis for assigning them real chemical identities. Accordingly, my mechanism is a process-level account of conversion, competing product formation, phase partitioning, and purification rather than a molecular mechanism.

Each batch began with 0.040 mol limiting reagent and 0.005 mol catalyst. Except for batch 1, the reaction used 0.040 L solvent, nitrogen, approximately atmospheric pressure, 600 rpm stirring, and 340 K. Reaction-stage HPLC was measured before quenching. The usual workup was quench, add 0.020 L aqueous phase and 0.040 L extractant, mix for 300 s, settle for 600 s, retain the organic phase, wash, dry, terminate, and perform the final assay. Thus the HPLC and final assay describe different physical domains: the HPLC describes the reaction mixture, while the final assay describes the selected, processed organic material.

2. Proposed reaction model

A minimal explanation is a network in which reactant R forms target P and one or more competing products B, while P and/or intermediates may also degrade:

R → P
R → B
P → degradation products

A useful phenomenological model would be

dR/dt = −(kP + kB)R,
dP/dt = kP R − kd P,
dB/dt = kB R + kd P,

where kP, kB, and kd depend on catalyst, solvent, temperature, and possibly concentration. Catalyst and solvent need not act independently; an interaction k(C,S,T) is plausible and is not distinguishable from independent effects with the available design.

Reaction-stage yield should approximately reflect conversion multiplied by selectivity, although the reported synthetic metrics include noise and need not obey that identity exactly. Temperature and time increase reaction progress, but the constrained objective depends on the relative rates of productive and competing pathways, not conversion alone.

The clearest reaction-stage lead was C1/S1 at 340 K for 3600 s. Across batches 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10, reaction-stage HPLC selectivity ranged from 0.494 to 0.542 and yield from 0.136 to 0.171. Their mean selectivity was about 0.520. Representative observations were:

• Batch 2: conversion 0.3001, selectivity 0.5027, yield 0.1571.
• Batch 6: conversion 0.2993, selectivity 0.5423, yield 0.1584.
• Batch 7: conversion 0.2839, selectivity 0.5405, yield 0.1477.
• Batch 8: conversion 0.2871, selectivity 0.5243, yield 0.1708.
• Batch 9: conversion 0.3233, selectivity 0.4944, yield 0.1645.
• Batch 10: conversion 0.3187, selectivity 0.5158, yield 0.1360.

The spread is compatible with process and measurement variation plus downstream-independent batch variation. HPLC standard uncertainties were approximately 0.012 for conversion and yield and 0.018 for selectivity. The repeated results nevertheless make C1/S1 a substantially better-supported reaction-stage lead than a conclusion based on one batch.

The initial diagonal screen changed my explanation. Batch 3 used C2/S2/X2 and gave reaction-stage conversion 0.3147 but selectivity only 0.2719 and yield 0.0802. Batch 4 used C3/S3/X3 and gave conversion 0.2518, selectivity 0.2855, and yield 0.0617. Batch 5 used C0/S1/X2 and gave relatively high conversion, 0.3510, but selectivity 0.3660 and yield 0.1116. These results showed that maximizing conversion was not equivalent to maximizing target production. They also suggested that C1 was useful, but the diagonal batches confounded catalyst, solvent, and extractant, so they cannot establish individual category effects.

3. Time–selectivity coupling

Batches 11 and 12 provide the nearest controlled time comparison. Both used C1/S0/X2 at 340 K with the standard one-wash workup; batch 11 reacted for 3600 s and batch 12 for 7200 s.

At the reaction stage, increasing time raised conversion from 0.1413 to 0.2482 and yield from 0.0985 to 0.1362. Selectivity changed from 0.4777 to 0.5032. At the final assay, recovery rose from 0.0189 to 0.0455, but purity fell from 0.8254 to 0.7430. The purity change is much larger than the declared final-assay purity standard uncertainty of 0.008.

My interpretation is that longer reaction increased the absolute target inventory but also increased the inventory of material that survived or interfered with the same workup. This need not mean reaction-stage selectivity worsened—the measured selectivity actually rose slightly. It could instead mean that later-forming impurities have partition behavior closer to P, that the impurity population changed with time, or that the organic phase became more difficult to purify. Thus reaction kinetics and workup selectivity are coupled through mixture composition.

The evidence supports the local statement that, for C1/S0 at 340 K, 7200 s improves recovery but violates the purity constraint. It does not establish a general kinetic law outside 3600–7200 s or for other material combinations.

4. Extraction and purification model

After quenching, the species distribute between aqueous and organic phases. For a species i with distribution coefficient Di, an equilibrium approximation is

fraction of i in organic ≈ Di Vo/(Di Vo + Va),

where Vo and Va are effective organic and aqueous volumes. Mixing controls approach to this distribution, settling enables phase selection, and separation discards the unselected inventory. The extractant categories plausibly alter DP relative to DB and DR.

A one-stage recovery model is

final recovery ≈ reaction target yield × extraction capture × phase-transfer retention × wash retention × drying/handling retention.

Purity instead depends on relative retention:

purity = retained target/(retained target + retained non-target solutes).

This distinction explains why a workup can increase purity while lowering recovery.

The most informative extractant comparison used repeated C1/S1 reactions with one wash:

• Batch 6, X0: stage yield 0.1584; final purity 0.7808 and recovery 0.0391.
• Batch 2, X1: stage yield 0.1571; final purity 0.7734 and recovery 0.0436.
• Batch 7, X2: stage yield 0.1477; final purity 0.7805 and recovery 0.0509.
• Batch 8, X3: stage yield 0.1708; final purity 0.7750 and recovery 0.0331.

X2 had the largest observed final recovery in this subset even though it did not have the largest measured reaction-stage yield. This is consistent with better target partitioning or retention under X2. However, the recovery differences are comparable to the final-assay recovery standard uncertainty of 0.01, and the reactions were repeated batches rather than a shared mixture split among extractants. Therefore X2 is a practical lead, not a securely identified causal optimum. X1, X0, and X3 cannot be sharply ranked from these data.

For batches 2–12, final recovery divided by reaction-stage HPLC yield ranged approximately from 0.15 to 0.49. I use this only as a rough process-retention diagnostic because the two instruments assay different states and the metrics are noisy. It nevertheless demonstrates that downstream handling was a major determinant of overall recovery.

5. Washing behavior

Batches 7, 9, and 10 used C1/S1/X2 but one, two, and three 0.040 L washes, respectively:

• One wash, batch 7: final purity 0.7805, recovery 0.0509.
• Two washes, batch 9: final purity 0.7971, recovery 0.0414.
• Three washes, batch 10: final purity 0.7627, recovery 0.0201.

The first additional wash was associated with a modest numerical purity increase and a recovery decrease. The third wash did not continue the purity improvement and produced much lower recovery. Reaction-stage yields differed among these batches (0.1477, 0.1645, and 0.1360), so the comparison is not a clean split-sample study. Final purity uncertainty was 0.008 and recovery uncertainty 0.01. I therefore do not infer a deterministic nonmonotonic washing law from three points. The defensible conclusion is that extra washes impose a real recovery risk and did not demonstrate a robust purity benefit. A single wash was the best-supported operating compromise.

6. Why final conversion approached unity

Final-assay conversion was approximately 0.98–1.00 in almost every batch even when reaction-stage HPLC conversion was only 0.14–0.35. I do not interpret this as continued near-quantitative reaction after quenching. The more plausible process explanation is selection bias: unreacted R was preferentially discarded into the aqueous or rejected material, so very little reactant remained in the assayed organic fraction. Final conversion is consequently a conditional composition metric for the retained phase, not evidence for whole-batch conversion.

This distinction is important. For example, batch 11 had reaction-stage conversion 0.1413 but final conversion 0.9827, while its recovery was only 0.0189. High final conversion coexisting with low recovery is exactly what is expected when purification removes most reactant and also loses much of the product.

7. Concentration anomaly

Batch 1 differed materially from the later standard process. It used C0/S0 at 350 K, 0.080 L reaction solvent, a concentration step before extraction, and another concentration after washing. Its reaction-stage HPLC gave conversion 0.2003, selectivity 0.3845, and yield 0.0687. The final assay reported purity 0.7976 but recovery 0.0000, despite a nonzero final yield estimate of 0.0159.

I treated this as evidence against concentration in this operating region. Possible explanations include disproportionate product loss during concentration, concentration-induced degradation or precipitation into an unselected domain, or a measurement/boundary effect near zero recovery. Because batch 1 also differed in solvent volume, temperature, and material categories, it does not identify the causal mechanism. It does show that the particular combined batch-1 process was unsuitable.

8. Final constrained interpretation

Batch 11 was the only completed batch whose final-assay point estimate clearly met purity ≥ 0.80: purity 0.8254, recovery 0.0189, process mass-balance error reported as 0, and final conversion 0.9827. Its recipe was C1, S0, and X2; 340 K for 3600 s; quench; 0.020 L aqueous addition; 0.040 L extraction; retain organic; one 0.040 L wash; dry; terminate. The purity margin above the threshold was about 0.025, compared with a declared purity standard uncertainty of 0.008.

Several batches offered higher recovery but were below the point-estimate purity constraint. Batch 7 had purity 0.7805 and recovery 0.0509. Batch 9 had purity 0.7971 and recovery 0.0414. Batch 12 had purity 0.7430 and recovery 0.0455. Batch 1 and batch 9 were close enough to 0.80 that uncertainty-aware replicate confirmation could conceivably change their classification, but no such replicate confirmation was available. The sealed recommendation therefore correctly favored observed compliance over a higher but formally sub-specification recovery.

9. Unidentifiable factors and alternatives

The campaign does not identify molecular structures, activation energies, true partition coefficients, or individual impurity species. Catalyst loading, reagent charge, atmosphere, pressure, stirring speed, aqueous volume, extraction volume, mixing time, and settling time were essentially fixed, so their effects cannot be estimated. Temperature was almost fixed at 340 K; batch 1 at 350 K was heavily confounded. Only one direct reaction-time comparison was made. The initial catalyst/solvent screen was categorical and confounded, and most later runs concentrated around C1/S1.

Plausible alternatives to my explanation include: batch-to-batch latent variation rather than material interactions; extractant-dependent assay response rather than true partitioning; formation of an unmeasured solid or interfacial product; wash-induced chemical transformation rather than simple partitioning; and phase selection that removes reactant more efficiently than product without changing chemistry. The public evidence cannot discriminate these mechanisms.

Overall, the world is best explained as a coupled optimization: catalyst, solvent, temperature, and time determine the target and impurity inventory; extractant and phase handling determine which inventory reaches the selected organic phase; washing changes target and impurity retention unequally; and the purity constraint forces operation on a low-recovery frontier. The strongest local rule supported by the campaign is not “maximize conversion,” but “choose a reaction/workup pair whose impurity population is separable.” In the explored region, C1/S1 produced more target but remained slightly below the purity threshold, whereas the shorter C1/S0/X2 process sacrificed target formation and recovery to achieve compliant final purity.

payload.rationale: These recipes are substantial extrapolations from the campaign: they use solvent-S2, 400 K, only 0.00025 mol catalyst, smaller phase volumes, and—in Q07–Q12—only 0.002 mol reagent. The intervals therefore include much more model uncertainty than the stated final-assay noise. I treated reaction time as increasing target formation and recovery while eventually lowering final purity through additional co-produced or less readily separated material; this follows the batch-11 versus batch-12 pattern, where doubling time raised recovery from 0.0189 to 0.0455 but lowered purity from 0.8254 to 0.7430. For Q03–Q04, X2 receives a modest recovery advantage over X0 based on the repeated C1/S1 workups, but their intervals overlap because that extractant ranking was weak. For Q05–Q06, a larger organic volume is predicted to capture more target and also more non-target solute, giving higher recovery but lower purity. Q07–Q08 apply the observed wash tradeoff: washing should improve purity while losing some target. Q09–Q10 use the same total wash volume; two smaller stages are expected to remove impurities more efficiently, with a modest additional recovery penalty. Q11–Q12 differ only by concentration; I predict a small loss in recovery and purity after concentration because the campaign provided adverse, though confounded, evidence from batch 1. The low-charge recipes may achieve somewhat better fractional recovery because the catalyst-to-reagent ratio is much larger, but whether kinetics depend on that ratio or on catalyst concentration was not identifiable, so their recovery intervals are deliberately broad.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No instance-specific prior or nominal material-property dossier was supplied. The only starting information was that the material indices were anonymous categories, so all mechanistic claims were developed from campaign observations.

Supported within the explored region:
• C1/S1 was a reproducible reaction-stage lead at 340 K and 3600 s. Batches 2, 6–10 repeatedly gave HPLC selectivity 0.494–0.542 and yield 0.136–0.171. This repetition changed the initial category screen into a reasonably supported local relationship.
• Reaction progress and final quality were coupled but not interchangeable. In the closest time comparison, extending C1/S0/X2 from 3600 s in batch 11 to 7200 s in batch 12 increased reaction-stage conversion from 0.141 to 0.248 and final recovery from 0.0189 to 0.0455, while final purity fell from 0.825 to 0.743. This changed my judgment from treating longer reaction mainly as a route to more target to treating time as a recovery–purity tradeoff.
• Purification could remove reactant without preserving much target. Final conversion was near unity even when reaction-stage conversion was low; batch 11, for example, went from stage conversion 0.141 to final conversion 0.983 but retained only 0.0189 recovery. This supported a phase-selection explanation rather than continued quantitative reaction.
• Extra washing carried a recovery penalty. With C1/S1/X2, recovery decreased from 0.0509 in the one-wash batch 7 to 0.0414 in two-wash batch 9 and 0.0201 in three-wash batch 10.

Contradicted or weakened:
• A simple law that more washing monotonically increases purity was contradicted. Purity rose from 0.780 in batch 7 to 0.797 in batch 9, but fell to 0.763 in batch 10. Different reaction-stage yields and assay uncertainty prevent attributing all of this to washing, but monotonic improvement was not supported.
• Maximizing conversion was contradicted as an optimization rule. Batch 5 had stage conversion 0.351 but only 0.366 selectivity, while C1/S1 batches with conversion near 0.29–0.32 had selectivity near 0.50–0.54.
• Concentration as an automatically benign solvent-removal step was weakened by batch 1, which included pre- and post-extraction concentration and ended with reported recovery 0 despite purity 0.798. Because batch 1 also differed in solvent volume, temperature, and material categories, this was not a clean causal contradiction.
• X2 being definitively superior to all other extractants was not established. In the approximate C1/S1 comparison, X2 gave the highest recovery in batch 7 (0.0509), versus 0.0391 for X0 in batch 6, 0.0436 for X1 in batch 2, and 0.0331 for X3 in batch 8. Those differences were comparable to recovery uncertainty and were confounded by independent reaction batches.

Untested or only conjectural:
• The proposed differential equations for parallel target formation, byproduct formation, and degradation were not quantitatively identified.
• Arrhenius temperature dependence, catalyst-loading dependence, catalyst–solvent interactions, true distribution coefficients, and whether washing caused only partitioning or also chemical transformation remained untested.
• Product preference for the organic phase was inferred from retained product, not established by paired assays of both separated phases.
• Effects of pressure, atmosphere, stirring, mixing time, settling time, phase ratio, and reagent concentration were essentially untested because they were fixed or nearly fixed.

2. One discriminating experiment

I would run one C1/S1 reaction at 340 K for 3600 s, quench it, homogenize it, and divide it equally into two workup arms. Both arms would receive identical aqueous and organic volumes, mixing, settling, one wash, drying, transfer, and final assay; the only difference would be X0 versus X2. Volumes would be scaled so that phase ratios and reagent-equivalent loading were identical. A reaction-stage HPLC measurement before splitting would establish a common starting composition.

This split-batch design distinguishes the leading explanation—that X2 improves target partitioning or retention—from the alternative that the apparent X2 advantage arose from independent-batch reaction variability or assay noise.

• If X2 produced materially higher recovery at similar or higher purity, I would strengthen the partition-coefficient explanation and the ranking X2 > X0 for this mixture.
• If recoveries and purities were indistinguishable within measurement uncertainty, I would withdraw the extractant ranking and attribute most earlier differences among batches 6 and 7 to batch variation.
• If X2 increased recovery but decreased purity, I would revise the claim to a capture–selectivity tradeoff rather than general superiority.
• If X0 outperformed X2 on both metrics, the earlier ranking would be contradicted and interactions with uncontrolled batch composition would become the leading explanation.

3. Unused evidence, weak predictions, and goal effects

The raw characterization artifacts and detailed spectral traces were largely unused; decisions relied on processed HPLC and final-assay estimates. No GC, NMR, IR, MS, or UV–visible cross-validation was collected. The aqueous phase was never independently assayed after separation, so discarded target was inferred from mass-balance behavior rather than directly localized. I also did not use replicate final assays, randomized split-sample workups, or a systematic factorial model. The process-time, cost, safety, and raw peak-shape information received little weight because the assigned objective prioritized purity and recovery.

The least reliable sealed predictions are those for the new 400 K recipes, especially Q01–Q06: catalyst loading was twentyfold lower than in the campaign, solvent-S2 with C1 was not directly tested, and 400 K lay well outside the main 340 K evidence. Q07–Q12 are also uncertain because the 0.002 mol reagent charge was never studied and it is unknown whether fractional kinetics depend mainly on catalyst concentration or catalyst-to-reagent ratio. Predictions about phase-volume effects (Q05/Q06), staged washing (Q09/Q10), and concentration (Q11/Q12) were mechanistic extrapolations from little or confounded evidence. Their broad intervals reflect that limitation.

The operating recommendation is also locally rather than generally reliable. Batch 11 was selected because its purity point estimate, 0.825, was the only clear result above 0.80, but its recovery was only 0.0189 and it was not replicated. Batch 9 had much greater recovery, 0.0414, and purity 0.797, just below the threshold and within the stated purity uncertainty. Replication could therefore change the practical ranking.

The assigned goal materially affected evidence collection. Once C1/S1 appeared promising, later experiments concentrated on extractant identity and wash count rather than continuing a balanced catalyst–solvent–temperature design. The hard purity constraint also caused the final choice to favor batch 11 over higher-recovery but sub-specification batches 7, 9, and 12. Using one HPLC measurement per batch maximized broad campaign coverage but left no measurement budget for replicate assays or direct aqueous/organic mass-balance tests. This was a rational response to the goal, but it reduced mechanistic identifiability. There was no clear conflict between evidence and the formal selection rule; the main tension was between strict point-estimate compliance and the uncertainty surrounding near-threshold alternatives.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 11 is the only completed batch with observed final purity above the required 0.80 (0.8254) and retains measurable recovery (0.0189). Its approximately 0.025 purity margin is larger than the declared assay purity standard uncertainty (0.008). Higher-recovery batches 7 and 9 had point-estimate purities below specification, so they were not selected.
